title.en: Soni and Avi at the fair

text.en: Soni and Avi visit the Surajkund Fair, where craft stalls come from all over India. They make malas of beads, see beautiful rangolis and masks, and play a mirror game. Along the way they learn about shapes that look the same on both sides.

A man and a woman at a stall are making malas with beads. Soni and Avi make malas with 8 beads, 4 of one colour and 4 of another. Some of their malas look the same on both halves, and some do not. If the two halves match exactly, the mala is symmetrical. A mala with red, red, blue, blue, blue, blue, red, red is symmetrical, because the left half is the mirror of the right half. A mala with red, blue, blue, red, red, blue, red, red is not symmetrical, because the two halves are different. We can use 6 beads of one colour and 2 beads of another to make symmetrical malas, by putting 1 bead of the second colour on each side.
At the Tamil Nadu stall Amma makes a kolam in front of her hut. Many kolams, rangolis, pookalams and aipans have patterns that match on both sides. If we draw a line through the middle of a rangoli and the two sides are exactly the same, the rangoli is symmetrical. We can test it by tracing the rangoli on a paper and folding the paper along the line. If one half lies exactly on the other half, the pattern is symmetrical. Not all rangolis are symmetrical. Some have a different pattern on each side, and some have more than one line that splits them in two matching halves. We can complete a half-rangoli by drawing the other half on a dot grid, taking each dot and line to the same distance on the other side of the fold.
Soni makes a cat mask by folding a paper in half, drawing half a cat, cutting along the line and opening it. The two sides are the same, so the mask is symmetrical. Avi's mask had its eye holes on only one side, so it was not symmetrical, and he could see with one eye. A painter drew half of a picture and said the other half is just the same. A mirror shows the other half. A trick like this works for symmetrical things, so he should draw things that are not symmetrical. In the mirror game, one child places counters on one side of a line and the other places counters as a mirror image on the other side. We can check by putting a mirror on the line.
Many things around us are symmetrical, such as a butterfly, a leaf, a kite and the letters A, H and M. Some things are not symmetrical, such as a hand, a shoe pair seen as one shoe, or the letter F. To check, imagine a line through the middle and see whether both sides would match exactly if folded.

problem.en: A mala has beads in the order red, red, blue, blue, blue, blue, red, red. Is it symmetrical?

text.en: Split the mala in the middle.

why.en: The line of symmetry is in the middle.

text.en: The left half is red, red, blue, blue and the right half is blue, blue, red, red read the other way.
Yes, each bead matches its mirror partner.

problem.en: How do we test if a rangoli is symmetrical using tracing paper?

text.en: Trace the rangoli.

why.en: Make a copy of the pattern.

text.en: Fold the paper so one half falls on the other.
If every line matches exactly, it is symmetrical.

problem.en: Why could Avi see only with one eye in his mask?

text.en: His mask had holes only on one side.

why.en: The holes were not the same on both sides.

text.en: So his mask was not symmetrical.
He should have cut both eye holes in the same positions on each half.

why.en: Folding first keeps the sides equal.

prompt.en: Explain what it means for a shape to be symmetrical.

requiredIdeas.en: A fold line or mirror line
One half lies on the other
Examples like a butterfly or a mask

commonMisconceptions.en: A symmetrical shape must be round

points.en: A shape is symmetrical if the two halves match exactly.
We can test with a fold or a mirror.
Rangolis, malas, masks and butterflies can be symmetrical.
A mirror image is the same picture on the other side of a line.
